analysis.one_liner: Bars companies convicted of serious federal crimes from political spending for six years.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 2017 and referred to the House Administration Committee, where it sat until the 115th Congress ended without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, corporations can spend money to influence federal, state, and local elections. This bill would strip that right for six years from any corporation convicted of conspiracy against the United States or another felony involving dishonesty or breach of trust, or that settles such charges with the Justice Department through a deferred-prosecution or nonprosecution agreement requiring a payment of $1 million or more.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would see six years of election spending removed from companies found guilty of federal crimes like fraud or conspiracy, or that paid $1 million or more to settle such charges with the Justice Department.

how_it_helps.text: Adds a new section to the Federal Election Campaign Act making it unlawful for a 'criminal corporation' — or its political action fund — to make campaign contributions, independent expenditures, or electioneering communications for six years after conviction or a qualifying settlement.

Defines a criminal corporation as one convicted of conspiracy to defraud the United States or another felony involving dishonesty or breach of trust, or one that resolved such charges through a deferred-prosecution or nonprosecution agreement with a payment of $1 million or more.
The ban covers spending in federal, state, and local elections, applying to all corporate political disbursements to the extent they are currently lawful.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations that commit serious federal crimes or buy their way out with $1 million-plus settlements would lose their ability to bankroll election campaigns for six years; companies would also bear the cost of compliance tracking.

drawbacks.text: The definition is narrow: it reaches only felony convictions or dishonesty/breach-of-trust offenses, so most corporations that settle regulatory or civil enforcement actions would keep spending freely; critics of campaign-finance limits could also argue it penalizes an entity that has already paid its criminal sentence.
Six-year bans on corporate speech raise First Amendment objections under the Supreme Court's Citizens United line of cases, which a court challenge could test.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is cleaner elections: companies caught committing serious federal crimes lose the power to influence the very elections that set their regulators. The cost falls on those companies and their shareholders, and the narrow definition limits how many firms would actually be affected. The main risk is a constitutional challenge to restricting corporate election speech.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Administration Committee on the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the bill in the House on January 24, 2017, joined by Rep. Eric Swalwell of California.
The same day, it was referred to the Committee on House Administration, which controls campaign-finance and election bills in the House.
The committee never reported the bill, and no vote of any kind was taken on it before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
The bill's only cosponsor was a single House Democrat.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations with criminal records or large Justice Department settlements keep their ability to spend on elections, and the House majority that declined to act on campaign-finance reform avoided a fight over it.

for.name: Rep. Keith Ellison
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban six years of campaign spending by corporations convicted of serious federal crimes or paying $1 million-plus settlements.

for.name: Rep. Eric Swalwell
for.what_they_did: Joined Ellison as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never held a hearing, marked it up, or reported it out, leaving it to die at the end of the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors and the sole cosponsor were House Democrats, and no votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of broader support or opposition was never tested on the record.

industries.industry: Corporations convicted of federal felonies or paying $1 million-plus deferred-prosecution settlements
industries.note: The bill strips these companies of the right to make campaign contributions, independent expenditures, and electioneering communications for six years after conviction or settlement. That matters for voters because such companies — typically large banks, drug makers, and defense contractors facing federal fraud charges — would no longer be able to fund campaigns for the officials who oversee their regulators.

Separate segregated funds run by criminal corporations would face the same six-year spending ban, and companies would need compliance systems to track convictions and settlements. The affected universe would be small but the covered groups are heavy political spenders.
